10. The Court of appeal below, on the other hand, relied upon the testimony of DW 1 and observed that he did not have sexual relationship with the plaintiff No.1 and therefore, the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 were not his legitimate children and that DWs 2, 3, 5 and 6 corroborated him who are neutral witnesses. The Court of appeal below further held that the Family Court wrongly relied upon section 112 of the Evidence Act which has no manner of application for deciding the said dispute. As regards the decision as to sexual relationship there is no legal evidence in support of the same and based upon the evidence of DWs 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 as corroborative evidence of DW 1. It can be proved by DW 1 by adducing reliable evidence but he has failed to proved the same. The evidence of DWs 2-6 cannot be taken as corroborative evidence, it being none other than the couple can lead evidence whether or not they had access at the time of conception. It is only the husband and wife who could say whether they had co-habitation or not. If any child is born during the subsistence of marriage, the presumption is that the child was born in the wedlock, unless the person who denied the said fact proved that he had no co- habitation with his wife; the onus heavily lay upon him. 

 12. This section creates in favour of a child both born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his/her mother and the father, a conclusive presumption of legitimacy, in the absence of evidence of non access between the parents. This provision is based on the English rule that the child born in wedlock should be treated as the child of the man who was then the husband of the mother unless it is shown that he had no access to the mother at the time of conception. When a child was born during the wedlock, there is an initial presumption of the legitimacy; in other words" that the husband had intercourse with the wife at the time when the child must have been conceived. Presumption is rebuttable one and may be deviated by showing non access; but once access of or intercourse by, the husband is proved, no evidence can be allowed to show that the child is not the child of the husband. The words "access" and "non-access" mean the existence or non existence of opportunities for sexual intercourse. The access between husband and wife viewed with reference to the result, namely, the procreation of children. It is immaterial how soon after the marriage the child is born; and the presumption applies although the birth occurred so soon after the marriage that the child must have been begotten before it or even if the mother was visibly pregnant at the time of marriage. There is ordinary period of gestation of 280 days, a child born within less than this period of the marriage will, in the absence of evidence of non access, be presumed under this provision to be legitimate. Reference in this connection is the case of Sibt Mohammad vs Mohammad Hameed, ILR 48 Allahabad 625. 

 13. There is a presumption that every person is legitimate and there is presumption that a person is that legitimate issue of a particular person, unless a foundation for it is laid under section 112. But once the validity of the marriage is proved, it is unnecessary to establish affirmatively that the child is illegitimate. If, therefore, it is not proved that the child was born of the body of the wife or that it was born during the marriage or that the father was alive at the date of conception or that the child was born within 280 days of the dissolution of the marriage, no presumption of legitimacy will arise. To raise the presumption of legitimacy under this provision it must be proved that at the date of birth of the child a valid marriage existed between the mother of the child and the father. Where a man and woman are proved to have lived together as husband and wife the law will presume, unless the contrary be clearly proved, that they were living together in consequence of a valid marriage and not in a state of concubinage, provided a legal marriage was possible between them. The presumption is always in favour of legitimacy. Hence the evidence of non access is on the party alleging it. 

 14. Therefore, it is highly unsafe to pass a finding of adultery and illegitimacy in the absence of clear and satisfactory evidence. If marriage has been dissolved by divorce or by the death of the husband and within 280 days of such dissolution but the mother remains unmarried a child is born to her, it will be presumed to be legitimate. The presumption created by section 112 of the Evidence Act is conclusive but, in fact, it is not a conclusive presumption, inasmuch as it is liable to be rebutted by proof of non access at the time of conception. The burden of proof of non access is of course on the person who alleges it. To rebut the presumption of legitimacy it is competent to negative the fact of sexual intercourse between the husband and wife during the time, when according to course of nature, the husband can have been the father of the child. If the Court is satisfied that the husband had, or from the circumstances of time, place and health could have had, intercourse with his wife at the necessary time, the presumption will not be rebutted by proof that she also had connection with other men, as the law will not in that case allow a balance of evidence as to who was most likely to be the father of the child. 

 "The rules of Mohammaden Law relating to acknowledgment by a Mohammaden of another as his son are rules of the substantive law of inheritance. Such an acknowledgment, unless certain impediments exist, confers upon the person acknowledged the status of a legitimate son capable of inheriting where there is no proof of legitimate birth or of illegitimate birth, and the paternity of a child is unknown, in the sense that no specific person is shown to be the father, then the acknowledgment of him by another who claims him as his son affords a conclusive presumption that he is the legitimate child of acknowledger, and places him in that category."
